idiom_name: enum with data as the hierarchy + sqlx::Type for the discriminative column
implementation_notes: Rust has no inheritance, so the hierarchy becomes one enum whose variants carry the subtype fields - the idiomatic replacement for a class hierarchy - while the table keeps the union of columns plus a tag column. sqlx's derivable Type trait maps that tag: with #[repr(iN)] the integer discriminant is used (for an INT column), otherwise the variant names are used and must match a textual SQL type (VARCHAR/TEXT), and #[sqlx(rename_all = ...)] controls the casing; sqlx::FromRow then builds the row struct, and the match that assembles the enum variant is the mapper. Diesel and sqlx do not implement STI, so nothing generates the mapping; the exhaustive match plus a CHECK constraint on the tag column are what stand in for the missing schema guarantee.
pitfalls: The tag decode is only as strict as the type you choose: with String/&str an unknown value becomes an ordinary string, so the exhaustive match (returning an error, never unreachable!()) is the only place a mapping error can be caught.
Option<T> cannot distinguish 'this column does not belong to the subtype' from 'the value is NULL'; a CHECK constraint or a per-kind view is the only real guard.
A Rust enum with data does not map 1:1 to a flat table - flattening variants into columns is the mapper's job, and adding a variant means changing the enum, the row struct and the SQL together.
sqlx's query macros verify SQL against the database at compile time, but not your discriminator logic; a column renamed in the schema can still line up with the wrong Option field.
